meta.moduleTitle: 17.2 KINS 4403: Physiological Responses to Acute Exercise

pages.title: Part 1: Anaerobic Capacity and Glycolytic Limitations
pages.readingHtml:
Anaerobic Metabolic Capacity in Children

Pediatric exercise physiology research demonstrates that children possess a distinctly limited ability to perform sustained high-intensity anaerobic activities. While young children can execute short, explosive bursts of movement with efficacy similar to adults, their capacity to maintain high power output for durations spanning $15\text{ s}$ to $2\text{ min}$ is significantly constrained. This limitation stems from a lower glycolytic capacity in pediatric skeletal muscle.

High-Energy Phosphate Stores vs. Glycolytic Energy Systems

To understand pediatric anaerobic energy production, exercise physiologists evaluate the distinct metabolic energy pathways:

  • ATP-PCr Energy System: Children's resting skeletal muscle stores of adenosine triphosphate ($\text{ATP}$) and phosphocreatine ($\text{PCr}$) are comparable to those observed in adults. Consequently, high-intensity exercise efforts lasting less than $10$ to $15\text{ s}$ in duration—such as brief sprints or vertical jumps—are not compromised in pediatric populations.
  • Anaerobic Glycolytic System: Significant anaerobic deficits emerge during high-intensity exertion that taxes anaerobic glycolysis ($15\text{ s}$ up to $2\text{ min}$). Pediatric skeletal muscle contains lower resting glycogen stores, measuring approximately $50\%$ to $60\%$ of adult resting baseline concentrations.

Enzymatic Bottlenecks and Lactate Dynamics

Following maximal and supramaximal exercise, children produce significantly lower concentrations of lactate in both skeletal muscle tissue and systemic circulation compared to adults. This blunted lactate response is mediated by specific enzymatic and metabolic factors:

  • Phosphofructokinase (PFK) Deficiency: Children exhibit lower concentrations and reduced activity of phosphofructokinase ($\text{PFK}$), the rate-limiting enzyme responsible for catalyzing early glycolytic reactions.
  • Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) Activity Deficit: Pediatric skeletal muscle displays markedly reduced activity of lactate dehydrogenase ($\text{LDH}$)—approximately $3.5\text{-fold}$ lower than adult LDH activity levels. This enzymatic bottleneck severely restricts the reduction of pyruvate to lactate.
  • Lactate Kinetics and Aerobic Compensation: Lower post-exercise blood lactate concentrations in children also reflect their lower relative muscle mass (producing less total pyruvate), higher systemic lactate clearance rates, and a greater relative reliance on aerobic mitochondrial metabolism during intense exertion.

Clinical / Coaching Application

When designing conditioning drills for pre-pubertal athletes, coaches must recognize that children cannot sustain intense anaerobic efforts lasting $30\text{ s}$ to $2\text{ min}$ due to lower PFK and LDH activity. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) for children should utilize brief work bouts ($<10\text{ s}$) with generous recovery intervals to rely on intact ATP-PCr kinetics and rapid oxidative recovery, avoiding excessive glycolytic fatigue.

pages.title: Part 2: Anaerobic Power Development and Developmental Scaling
pages.readingHtml:
Laboratory and Field Assessment of Pediatric Anaerobic Power

Anaerobic performance capability increases progressively throughout childhood and adolescence. Exercise physiologists quantify anaerobic power using both laboratory cycle ergometry and functional field tests:

  • Wingate Anaerobic Power Test: A $30\text{-s}$, all-out maximal cycling sprint evaluating peak power output (highest mechanical power in first $5\text{ s}$) and mean anaerobic power (average power sustained over $30\text{ s}$). Children achieve significantly lower absolute peak and mean power outputs compared to adults.
  • Margaria Step-Running Test: A functional field test evaluating stair-climbing sprint speed to measure maximal anaerobic power output scaled to body weight.

Allometric Scaling and Power Velocity Curves

Because absolute mechanical power is strongly influenced by total body size and muscle mass, exercise scientists adjust power output relative to body weight ($\text{W/kg}$). As illustrated in Figure 17.8, even when peak power is statistically adjusted for body mass:

  • Preteenagers ($9\text{--}10\text{ years of age}$) display exceptionally low relative peak power outputs compared to teenagers and adults.
  • Teenagers ($14\text{--}15\text{ years of age}$) achieve relative power outputs much closer to adult reference values (mean age $21\text{ years}$), demonstrating that anaerobic power development accelerates during pubertal maturation beyond simple body size expansion.

Bar-Or's Developmental Trajectories (Ages 9 to 16)

Bar-Or summarized the developmental trajectories of aerobic and anaerobic characteristics in boys and girls from ages $9$ through $16$, expressing performance relative to the $18\text{-year-old}$ adult criterion baseline ($100\%$ of adult capacity; Figure 17.9):

  • Aerobic Fitness Trajectory: Aerobic fitness (expressed as $\text{VO}_2\text{max}$ scaled to body mass) remains virtually constant in boys across ages $9$ to $16$. In girls, relative $\text{VO}_2\text{max}$ gradually declines from $12$ to $16\text{ years}$. Notably, $9\text{-}$ to $12\text{-year-old}$ girls possess higher relative aerobic fitness than the $18\text{-year-old}$ female adult baseline, reaching approximately $110\%$ of the reference adult value.
  • Anaerobic Capacity Trajectory: For both boys and girls, relative anaerobic capacity increases steadily and continuously from $9$ through $15\text{ years}$ of age, reflecting structural muscle growth, enzymatic maturation, and neural motor unit recruitment gains.

Clinical / Coaching Application

When assessing fitness in youth sports, coaches must avoid comparing raw, unadjusted power test scores across different age brackets. Because anaerobic power accelerates dramatically during pubertal maturation, scaling power output to body mass ($\text{W/kg}$) allows coaches to track true neuromuscular development and distinguish between early-maturing and late-maturing athletes.

pages.title: Part 3: Endocrine Responses and Substrate Utilization
pages.readingHtml:
Endocrine Regulation of Exercise Metabolism

Physical activity stimulates the release of metabolic regulatory hormones that mobilize carbohydrates and lipids for ATP re-synthesis. In children, these exercise-induced endocrine surges directly interact with ongoing somatic growth and physiological maturation:

  • Growth Hormone (GH) & IGF-1 Axis: Exercise represents a potent stimulus for the growth hormone ($\text{GH}$) and insulin-like growth factor $1$ ($\text{IGF-1}$) axis. High-intensity exercise in children triggers dramatic transient peaks in circulating $\text{GH}$ concentrations, modifying the normal diurnal pulsatile secretion of growth hormone.
  • Insulin and Stress Hormone Dynamics: Pediatric research indicates that insulin sensitivity and insulin responses to exercise vary across pubertal stages and between biological sexes. Furthermore, children exhibit a heightened sympathoadrenal stress response during acute exercise compared to adults.

Relative Hypoglycemia and Hepatic Glycogenolysis

At the onset of acute physical exertion, children frequently experience a transient relative hypoglycemia (a temporary drop in blood glucose concentration). This glucose regulation pattern stems from specific pediatric physiological constraints:

  • Lower resting muscle glycogen stores ($50\%\text{--}60\%$ of adult levels).
  • An immature capacity for hepatic glycogenolysis (liver glycogen breakdown into glucose).
  • Constrained endogenous glucose production during initial exercise transitions.

Pediatric Substrate Utilization Profiles

To compensate for lower glycolytic enzyme capacity and constrained hepatic glucose release, children display a unique metabolic fuel profile during physical exertion:

  • Enhanced Fat Oxidation: Children rely more heavily on fat oxidation as their primary fuel source during submaximal exercise compared to adults, preserving limited carbohydrate stores.
  • Exogenous Glucose Utilization: Pediatric populations exhibit a relatively high rate of exogenous glucose oxidation during exercise, efficiently oxidizing consumed dietary carbohydrates to offset reduced endogenous liver glucose output.
  • Pubertal Transition in Fuel Selection: Throughout pubertal maturation, substrate utilization shifts systematically. Adolescents display a progressive decline in relative fat oxidation rates and a corresponding increase in carbohydrate oxidation, gradually adopting adult metabolic fuel profiles.

Clinical / Coaching Application

Due to an immature capacity for hepatic glycogenolysis and lower resting muscle glycogen, young athletes are susceptible to relative hypoglycemia during prolonged physical activity. Providing easily digestible carbohydrate beverages during extended sports practices effectively supports energy demands, as children possess a high capacity for exogenous glucose oxidation.

glossary.def: The maximal capacity of the anaerobic glycolytic energy system to re-synthesize ATP during high-intensity exercise.
The key rate-limiting enzyme of anaerobic glycolysis that catalyzes the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.
An enzyme that catalyzes the reversible conversion of pyruvate to lactate; exhibits significantly lower (~3.5-fold) activity in pediatric skeletal muscle.
A 30-second all-out maximal cycle ergometer sprint test used to evaluate peak power output and mean anaerobic power.
A field test of anaerobic power measuring maximal energy expenditure during staircase sprinting.
The highest mechanical power generated during a short-duration all-out exercise test, typically occurring within the first 5 seconds of the Wingate test.
The average mechanical power sustained over the entire duration of an anaerobic power test, such as the 30-second Wingate test.
The endocrine pathway comprising pituitary growth hormone and liver-derived insulin-like growth factor 1, which regulates somatic growth and responds acutely to physical exercise.
The enzymatic breakdown of glycogen stored in the liver into glucose for release into the bloodstream to maintain blood glucose homeostasis.
A transient drop in blood glucose concentration observed at the onset of exercise in children due to lower muscle glycogen stores and immature hepatic glycogenolysis.
The metabolic breakdown and oxidation of dietary carbohydrates consumed immediately before or during physical exercise.
The relative proportion of carbohydrate versus fat oxidized by skeletal muscle to synthesize ATP during physical exertion.
